title: Benedict
hook: a young man flees Rome's chaos for a cave, then writes a rule of life for monks
carry: listen, with the ear of the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brigid of Kildare, and your line was mary of the gael. What useful thing did you give away, or set by the door? Day seven hundred eighty-six.

Bread comes down on a rope, with a little bell tied on so the man below will know it's coming. He's living alone in a cave in the hills, and a monk nearby keeps him fed. Not long before, he was a student in Rome, from a good family. He looked around at the city, and at the students around him, and was afraid that if he stayed, he'd go over the same edge they were going over. So he walked away from his books and his prospects. The young man is Benedict. Today: Benedict.
screen: `BREAD ON A ROPE, AND A BELL.`

segments.voice: We know his early life from Gregory the Great, a pope who wrote it down in a book of stories called the Dialogues. Gregory's Benedict is full of wonders. But the thing Benedict himself left behind is quieter: a Rule, a short book about how monks should live together. Here is how it begins, in its Latin: Ausculta, o fili. Listen, my son, to the master's teaching, and incline the ear of your heart. Listen is the first word. Not obey. Not work. Listen. And not just with the ears. With the ear of the heart. The Rule keeps turning to scripture. Early on it takes up a psalm, in the King James words: "To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your heart." Then it gets practical. When to pray, through the day and the night. When to eat, and how much, and when to keep silent. How to choose an abbot, and why the abbot should call everyone to counsel, even the youngest, because, the Rule says, the Lord often shows what is better to the younger. How to welcome guests: each one received as Christ, because Christ will say, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." The Rule hopes, it says, to set down nothing harsh, nothing burdensome. It calls itself a little rule for beginners. One thing gets repeated about Benedict that isn't his: the motto ora et labora, pray and work. It's a fair summary of the life, but those words aren't in the Rule. What's in the Rule is the first word. Benedict built a whole way of living on it, and communities that follow his Rule, Catholic, Anglican and others, still read from it together.

Here's the practice: find one line of a rule for your own day. Settle, and breathe. Start where Benedict starts: listen. What is the ear of your heart hearing about how your days are going? Maybe it's more sleep. Maybe one meal without a screen. Maybe a few quiet minutes in the morning. Let one simple line come. Keep it short and gentle: nothing harsh, nothing burdensome. If you pray, you can offer that line to God. If you don't, just hold it, and get ready to write it down. The bell holds the time.
Benedict. The young man who left Rome for a cave, and wrote a rule of life that begins with one word: listen.
Your line: listen, with the ear of the heart. Today, write your one line down where you'll see it tomorrow morning, and keep it once. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns, in Catholic, Anglican and other communities, live by the Rule of Benedict and read from it together, and some lay Christians follow its pattern of prayer, work and hospitality as oblates.

notes: Gregory, Dialogues 2, prologue and ch. 1: sent to Rome to study, saw many falling into vice, withdrew; the cave at Subiaco (not named); the monk Romanus lowered bread on a rope with a bell. Paraphrased; confirm.

Rule, prologue: 'Ausculta, o fili, praecepta magistri, et inclina aurem cordis tui'; Psalm 95 ('hodie si vocem eius audieritis, nolite obdurare corda vestra'); 'nothing harsh, nothing burdensome'. Ch. 3: the Lord often reveals what is better to the younger. Ch. 53: guests received as Christ, citing Matthew 25:35. Ch. 73: 'this little rule for beginners'. Chapter numbers not spoken. Confirm.
'Ora et labora' does not appear in the Rule; it is a later motto. Confirm the myth item.
No dates or counts (e.g. number of chapters, Monte Cassino) stated, under the claims rule. 'Communities that follow his Rule, Catholic, Anglican and others, still read from it together': confirm.
Practice and carry ask for one line of a personal daily rule; nothing prescribed.
Editor: hook now opens on the bread and bell instead of another 'A young man...' opener (screens reordered to match); fixed the garbled 'short enough to keep and gentle enough to keep' line.
Audit: added Rule ch. 64 (choosing an abbot) to sources, since the teach mentions it. Note: the oldest manuscripts read 'Obsculta'; 'Ausculta' is the common form. Keeper may choose.
